deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft for Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854). Three unrelated blocks appear on it.

(A) Top lines. These finish the continuity argument from the previous and next pages: if the change of x is made small enough, the change of F(x) can be made as small as desired. In modern terms, F is continuous.

(B) Main column: absolute versus conditional convergence and the rearrangement theorem.
- Riemann splits series into two classes. The first class stays convergent when every term is made positive (absolutely convergent). The second class does not (conditionally convergent).
- First-class series may be rearranged freely. The value of a second-class series depends on the order of its terms.
- Proof. Let a_1, a_2, ... be the positive terms and -b_1, -b_2, ... the negative terms of a conditionally convergent series.
  - Both sum a_k and sum b_k must diverge. If both were finite, the series would converge absolutely. If only one were infinite, the series would diverge.
  - Given any C, take positive terms until the partial sum exceeds C, then negative terms until it falls below C, and repeat.
  - After each sign change, the distance from C is at most the term just before the last sign change.
  - Since a_k → 0 and b_k → 0 (implicit: because the original series converges), the deviations tend to 0. The rearranged series therefore converges to C.
- Commentary on the text:
  - Only first-class series obey the laws of finite sums and can be treated as the aggregate of their terms.
  - The 18th-century mathematicians overlooked this, mainly because power series are, apart from isolated values, in the first class.
  - The Fourier series is not necessarily in the first class. Hence its convergence cannot be derived from the law by which the terms decrease, as Dirichlet had tried in vain.

(C) Right column, three fragments.

(C1) Sawtooth function. Riemann defines (x) as the excess of x over the nearest integer, with value 0 (the mean of 1/2 and -1/2) when x is midway between two integers; n denotes an integer. This is the sawtooth function of his famous example f(x) = sum (nx)/n^2, an integrable function with a dense set of discontinuities.

(C2) Euler-factor computation. Note: the page itself gives no context for this fragment; the interpretation is mine.
- The terms p^(nu-1)(p-1)/p^(2nu) are phi(p^nu)/p^(2nu).
- Summing over nu >= 1 gives 1 + (p-1)/p^2 · 1/(1 - 1/p) = 1 + 1/p.
- Hence 1 + 1/p is the Euler factor of sum phi(n)/n^2, i.e. of zeta(s-1)/zeta(s) at s = 2.
- The separate line 'IV (p-1)/p^(nu+1)' is the density of integers divisible by exactly p^nu.
- My reading: the discontinuities of Riemann's example lie at x = m/(2n) with m coprime to 2n. There are about phi(n) of them for each n, each with a jump of order 1/n^2.
- So this looks like an estimate of the total jump mass, sum phi(n)/n^2. Its product, prod(1 + 1/p), diverges.
- This fits the half-legible top note about 'Die Gesammtmasse ... Sprünge'.

(C3) 'Third group' estimate for Riemann's first lemma. The lemma states: if sum A_n = f, then (F(x+2α) - 2F(x) + F(x-2α))/(4α^2) = sum A_n (sin nα/(nα))^2 → f as α → 0.
- Abel summation with A_n = ε_n - ε_{n-1} gives terms ε_n · [(sin((n-1)α)/((n-1)α))^2 - (sin nα/(nα))^2]. The third group is n > s, where s = floor(π/α) and |ε_n| < δ.
- Write the difference as:
  [sin^2((n-1)α) - sin^2(nα)]/(nα)^2 + sin^2((n-1)α)[1/((n-1)α)^2 - 1/(nα)^2].
- Using sin^2 A - sin^2 B = sin(A+B) sin(A-B), the first part is -sin((2n-1)α) sin α/(nα)^2.
- Since |sin α| <= α, the absolute value is < 1/((n-1)α)^2 - 1/(nα)^2 + 1/(n^2 α).
- Summing over n > s: the first part telescopes to 1/(sα)^2. The second part is < (1/α) sum_{n>s} 1/n^2 < 1/(sα).
- So the third group is < δ(1/(sα)^2 + 1/(sα)). Since sα → π, this becomes δ(1/π + 1/π^2), as on the page.
- The next page combines this with the second group (< δ) to get the bound δ(1 + 1/π + 1/π^2).
errors: Rearrangement proof: the claim that deviations go to 0 needs a_k, b_k → 0. Riemann states this ('zuletzt unendlich klein'). It is implicit from the convergence of the original series.
Third-group estimate: indices are shifted relative to the next page ((n-1, n) here versus (n, n+1) there). This is harmless.
The first-part telescoping bound uses 1/((n-1)α)^2 with n starting at s+1, giving 1/(sα)^2. This is consistent.
In the p-column, the line transcribed as 1+(p-1)/p(1/p^2+1/p^3...) must read 1+(p-1)(1/p^2+1/p^3+...) to equal 1+1/p. As transcribed it would give 1+1/p^2.

results.what: Classification of series into absolutely and conditionally convergent; any conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any prescribed C
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, Habilitationsschrift 1854 (published 1867); Dirichlet 1837 noted that rearrangement can change the value

results.what: Remark that Fourier series need not converge absolutely, so Dirichlet's approach via the law of decrease of the terms cannot work
Definition of the sawtooth function (x): distance to the nearest integer with sign, 0 at half-integers
results.modern_name: Sawtooth function in Riemann's example of an integrable function with dense discontinuities

results.what: Euler factor sum_nu phi(p^nu)/p^(2nu) = 1/p, i.e. the local factor 1+1/p of sum phi(n)/n^2, apparently used to gauge the total jump mass
results.modern_name: Euler product for sum phi(n)/n^s = zeta(s-1)/zeta(s)

results.what: Bound on the tail n > π/α of the Abel-summed series in the proof that the second symmetric difference quotient of F tends to sum A_n, giving δ(1/π + 1/π^2)
results.modern_name: Riemann's first lemma (Riemann summability) in the uniqueness theory of trigonometric series

deep.surprise_reason: Almost everything here is draft material for the published Habilitationsschrift: the rearrangement theorem, the critique of Dirichlet, the (x) function, and the Riemann-lemma estimate. The only unpublished fragment is a small Euler-product computation of 1+1/p, apparently gauging the total jump mass of his example function. This is mildly interesting but elementary.

checkable.asserts: Placeholder: with sα → π, the bound δ(1/(sα)^2 + 1/(sα)) tends to δ(1/π + 1/π^2)
Tail estimate sum_{n>s} 1/n^2 < 1/s used for the second part of the third-group bound

transcription_corrections: Right column line 3 should read 1+(p-1)(1/p^2+1/p^3+...), not 1+(p-1)/p(...), for consistency with 1+1/p.
Main text 'so lange positive Reihe' should be 'so lange positive Glieder'.

Third-group formula: the page writes the difference of (sin((n-1)α)/((n-1)α))^2 and (sin nα/(nα))^2, rewritten as [sin^2((n-1)α) - sin^2(nα)]/(nα)^2 plus a remainder. The bound is <δ(1/((n-1)α)^2 - 1/(nα)^2) + δ/(n^2 α).
Top margin note probably reads 'Die Gesammtmasse der zu ... Stelle zugehörigen Sprünge folgt also ...'. It is illegible in part, and the transcription 'Lösung' is doubtful.
